title: Research Bite 83 Classroom Disruptions
author: Craig Barton
summary: In this weekly Research Bite, Craig Barton breaks down a German eye-tracking study by Sylvia Gabel and colleagues in which 15 experienced teachers and 18 trainees watched an 80-second maths lesson containing several minor disruptions and one major one. Experts' gaze patterns were more predictable throughout, narrowed onto the disruptive student and neighbours when the disruption happened, then returned to a steady scan of the class more quickly than the trainees' did. The experts also noticed the eventual troublemaker earlier. Barton translates this into five practical moves: sweep the whole room after dealing with a disruption, check the students sitting near it, build quieter disengaged students into your scan, settle on a regular scanning route, and if you mentor, show trainees where you look. He closes with cautions about the small sample, the single short clip and the lack of significant group differences, and notes that nobody has shown that teaching novices to look this way improves their management.
points: Expert teachers looked straight at the disruption and quickly returned to a steady whole-class scan, while trainees' gaze stayed scattered before, during and after.
After addressing a disruption, make a deliberate sweep of every table, back corners included, before resuming the explanation.
Experts also checked the students seated near the disruptive pupil, apparently to judge whether the behaviour was spreading, which tells you how firmly to respond.
Trainees were drawn to students with hands up and those in the front row, whereas experts noticed a disengaged student early who later became the main disruptor.
The study is small and uses a single clip with no significant group differences, so the findings are trends and it is untested whether training novices to look this way improves management.
quotes: Expert teachers looked straight at the disruption, then quickly returned to a steady scan of the whole class. Trainees’ eyes kept wandering unpredictably before, during and after.
Good monitoring means returning to your normal scanning routine once you've dealt with a disruption.

Once you’ve dealt with a disruption, sweep the whole room before carrying on. In the study, expert teachers’ eyes went straight to the disruptive student, then quickly returned to their regular pattern of scanning the class.

After the disruption, the experts’ eyes moved repeatedly between the disruptive student and the classmates sitting near him. The authors suggest experts are checking whether the behaviour is spreading to the people nearby.
The experts noticed a disengaged student early on who later became the main source of disruption.
Settle on a regular route for scanning the room. The experts’ looking followed a more predictable path from one student to the next, which the authors link to experience and well-practised habits.
Watch a short lesson clip with a trainee, pause just after a disruption, and ask where they would look next. Then explain where you would look and why.

Only 33 teachers took part, watching a single 80-second clip of a class they didn’t know, from a screen. The one statistical test reported found no significant group differences, so the patterns are trends.
